title: How Accurate Are IMF Growth Forecasts?
text: well International Monetary Fund (IMF) predict real GDP growth, forecast accuracy change prediction made advance? Forecast quality matters governments, businesses, researchers use IMF’s World Economic Outlook (WEO) inform decisions. Earlier evaluations include Timmermann (2007) Genberg Martinez (2014). article uses econdatasets::ed_get() download WEO vintages, match forecasts latest available estimates growth, describe absolute forecast errors horizons one five years. exercise measures accuracy, whether forecasts systematically - underestimate growth: taking absolute values removes direction error.

title: How Accurate Are IMF Growth Forecasts?
text: WEO vintage identified publication year release (Spring Fall). request columns needed analysis, underlying economic_outlook table large. keep real GDP growth series (NGDP_RPCH), country identifiers three uppercase letters, nonmissing values. Filtering series identifier avoids problems caused changes variable labels time. three-letter country-code restriction drops regional world aggregates, whose numeric identifiers consistently padded across vintages. vintage_key orders Spring Fall within year.
code: library(econdatasets) library(dplyr) library(forcats) library(ggplot2) library(fixest)  weo <- ed_get(   "imfweo",   "economic_outlook",   columns = c(     "entity_id",     "entity_name",     "series_id",     "year",     "value",     "publication_year",     "publication_release"   ),   quiet = TRUE )  growth <- weo |>   filter(     series_id == "NGDP_RPCH",     grepl("^[A-Z]{3}$", entity_id),     !is.na(value)   ) |>   mutate(     release_order = if_else(publication_release == "Fall", 1L, 0L),     vintage_key = 2L * publication_year + release_order   ) |>   select(-series_id, -release_order)

title: How Accurate Are IMF Growth Forecasts?
text: country target year, use GDP-growth value reported recent WEO vintage comparison outcome. forecast’s horizon target year minus publication year: 2020 release forecasting 2023 growth three-year horizon. retain horizons one five years, exclude target years less two years latest publication year comparison outcomes time mature. join excludes 239 eligible forecasts country-year pairs outcome latest vintage. Examples affected countries include Eritrea (ERI), Syrian Arab Republic (SYR), Kosovo (UVK), Yemen, Republic (YEM), Republic Yemen (YEM). missing country-year match, necessarily evidence country longer exists; differences historical coverage can also produce missing outcomes. absolute forecast error abs(actual - forecast), measured percentage points real GDP growth. example, forecast 3% outcome 1% imply absolute error 2 percentage points. latest vintage useful, consistently defined benchmark, historical growth figures may still revised; immutable final outcomes.
code: latest_vintage <- growth |>   filter(vintage_key == max(vintage_key)) |>   distinct(publication_year, publication_release)  actuals <- growth |>   filter(vintage_key == max(vintage_key)) |>   select(entity_id, year, actual = value)  eligible <- growth |>   mutate(horizon = year - publication_year) |>   filter(     between(horizon, 1, 5),     year <= latest_vintage$publication_year - 2   )  unmatched_forecasts <- eligible |>   anti_join(actuals, join_by(entity_id, year))  unmatched <- nrow(unmatched_forecasts) unmatched_examples <- unmatched_forecasts |>   distinct(entity_id, entity_name) |>   arrange(entity_id) |>   slice_head(n = 5)  predictions <- eligible |>   inner_join(     actuals,     join_by(entity_id, year),     relationship = "many-to-one"   ) |>   transmute(     entity_id,     entity_name,     year,     publication_year,     publication_release = factor(       publication_release,       levels = c("Spring", "Fall")     ),     vintage = fct_reorder(       paste(publication_year, publication_release),       vintage_key     ),     horizon,     forecast = value,     actual,     forecast_error = abs(actual - forecast)   )

title: How Accurate Are IMF Growth Forecasts?
text: first count country-forecast observations, countries represented, publication vintages, target-year range. Multiple releases forecast horizons can contribute observations country target year, independent country-year observations. Forecast sample analysis contains 25,779 forecasts 195 countries across 34 vintages. covers target years 2008-2024; counts describe matched sample rather every observation downloaded WEO table. Distribution forecasts, outcomes, absolute errors median absolute error 1.8 percentage points; 95th percentile 10.36 percentage points. difference indicates forecasts miss latest growth estimate substantially typical forecast. signed forecast actual growth rates can negative, absolute forecast errors .
code: sample_summary <- predictions |>   summarize(     observations = n(),     countries = n_distinct(entity_id),     vintages = n_distinct(vintage),     target_years = paste(range(year), collapse = "-")   )  knitr::kable(sample_summary, caption = "Forecast sample") summarize_variable <- function(x) {   tibble::tibble(     n = sum(!is.na(x)),     mean = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),     sd = sd(x, na.rm = TRUE),     q05 = quantile(x, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),     q25 = quantile(x, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),     median = median(x, na.rm = TRUE),     q75 = quantile(x, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),     q95 = quantile(x, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)   ) }  descriptive_stats <- bind_rows(   forecast = summarize_variable(predictions$forecast),   actual = summarize_variable(predictions$actual),   forecast_error = summarize_variable(predictions$forecast_error),   .id = "variable" )  knitr::kable(   descriptive_stats,   digits = 2,   caption = "Distribution of forecasts, outcomes, and absolute errors" )

what: How large are errors at different horizons?
title: How Accurate Are IMF Growth Forecasts?
text: following table reports mean absolute error (MAE) median absolute error separately horizon. directly addresses whether IMF’s forecasts become less accurate future, keeping mind horizon may cover different mix years countries. Absolute forecast errors horizon (percentage points) mean absolute error 3.06 percentage points one-year horizon 3.35 five-year horizon. difference (five-year minus one-year) 0.29 percentage points. Errors thus larger five years one year, rise every intermediate step: four-year MAE 3.37 compared 3.35 five years. raw comparison hold target-year conditions sample composition constant. Distribution absolute forecast errors publication year release. display restricted errors 15 percentage points. box summarizes middle half errors one vintage, line median. distributions vary across publication years releases, reflecting changes forecasting conditions well sample composition. Extreme errors excluded display keep boxes readable; remain statistics regressions.
code: horizon_summary <- predictions |>   group_by(horizon) |>   summarize(     observations = n(),     mean_absolute_error = mean(forecast_error),     median_absolute_error = median(forecast_error),     .groups = "drop"   )  knitr::kable(   horizon_summary,   digits = 2,   caption = "Absolute forecast errors by horizon (percentage points)" ) predictions |>   ggplot(aes(     x = factor(publication_year),     y = forecast_error,     fill = publication_release   )) +   geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +   geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +   coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 15)) +   labs(     x = "Publication year",     y = "Absolute error (percentage points)",     fill = "Release"   ) +   theme_minimal() +   theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

title: How Accurate Are IMF Growth Forecasts?
text: compare horizons systematically, regress absolute forecast errors horizon indicators, using one-year horizon reference category controlling Spring versus Fall releases. Model 1 includes controls; Model 2 adds target-year fixed effects account shocks common forecasts targeting calendar year. Model 3 also adds country fixed effects, comparing forecasts within countries controlling target-year differences. Standard errors clustered country allow correlations among forecasts country. omit publication-year fixed effects: horizon equals target year minus publication year, including sets year effects make full set horizon comparisons unidentified. Absolute forecast error regressions; t-statistics shown positive horizon coefficient means larger expected absolute error one year within specification. Model 1, five-year coefficient 0.29 percentage points; Model 2 0.36. Model 2 horizon coefficients positive: longer-horizon forecasts remain less accurate average accounting common target-year shocks. Model 3, five-year horizon coefficient 0.44 percentage points Fall coefficient -0.06. 5% significance level, four horizon indicators remain statistically significant including country target-year fixed effects; Fall difference remains statistically significant. Fall coefficient -0.07 Model 1 -0.05 Model 2. negative coefficient means smaller absolute errors Spring forecasts, conditional included controls. Fall releases information available within publication year, regressions establish errors differ. coefficients describe associations, causal effects forecast horizon release timing.
code: setFixest_dict(c(   forecast_error = "Forecast Error",   horizon = "Horizon",   year = "Target Year",   entity_id = "Country",   publication_releaseFall = "Fall" ))  clusters <- ~entity_id  models <- list(   "Model 1" = feols(     forecast_error ~ i(horizon, ref = 1) + publication_release,     predictions,     vcov = clusters   ),   "Model 2" = feols(     forecast_error ~ i(horizon, ref = 1) + publication_release | year,     predictions,     vcov = clusters   ),   "Model 3" = feols(     forecast_error ~ i(horizon, ref = 1) + publication_release |       year + entity_id,     predictions,     vcov = clusters   ) )  model_3_tests <- summary(models[[3]])$coeftable horizon_p_values <- model_3_tests[paste0("horizon::", 2:5), 4] fall_p_value <- model_3_tests["publication_releaseFall", 4]  knitr::kable(   etable(models, coefstat = "tstat", tex = FALSE),   caption = "Absolute forecast error regressions; t-statistics shown" )
